highlights.text: a single core idea: **laying something flat over something else of its own kind, so as to cover it.**
*ṭabaq* = *ḥāl* (condition). He cites Q 84:19, *la-tarkabunna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq* — "you shall mount stage upon stage."
Shāhid: Imruʾ al-Qays on rain — a steady, long-fringed drizzle that is "a covering of the earth," seeking its mark and pouring.
breadth, expanse, spreading out.
a disease/ailment.
The sea (al-baḥr) is named for its istibḥār — its spreading out and vastness.
baḥartu l-nāqa = to slit a she-camel's ear; such a camel is the baḥīra. Pre-Islamic Arabs did this after her tenth birth, then left her unridden and unused.
tabaḥḥara l-rāʿī = the shepherd ranging over wide pasture (cited from a verse of Umayya)
balawtu: to try/test someone (he proved "the best of those tried")
buliya / ubtuliya bi-: to be tried or afflicted; baliyya / balwā: a calamity that befalls one
God tries the servant with a good or bad trial
Hence lā ubālīhi, "I do not reckon with him," from not troubling to inform oneself about him (Zuhayr: "she does not care")
Hadith: refuge is sought from the hardship of balāʾ — except a balāʾ that carries elevation of rank with God.
the hamzated form yields a single root: repelling / pushing away.
From this same idea of "knowing where the quarry is" comes دَرَى in the sense of knowing/perceiving: دَرَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I knew the thing"), أَدْرانِيهِ اللهُ ("God made me know it").
Ibn Fāris cites Q 10:16, {…nor would He have made you know of it} (walā adrākum bihi)
الدَّرِيئَة: the practice-ring for spear-thrusting (verse of ʿAmr)
f-r-sh as a single sound root whose core idea is smoothing something out and spreading it flat.
Base sense — spreading. فَرَشْتُ الفِرَاشَ ("I spread the bedding").
الفَرْش of livestock — animals fit only for slaughter and eating.
فَرَاش is the flying insect (moth/butterfly), so named for its lightness.
a line of Abū Duʾād describing a scout who "came running with the fluttering of the ostrich, at a sprint, the day already high."
On the saying "the child belongs to the firāsh," he reports that some took firāsh to mean the husband, while arguing that strictly the firāsh is the woman, since she is the one bedded
derives the root ف ر ض (f-r-ḍ) from the concrete idea of a notch or incision
He reads the Qur'anic naṣīban mafrūḍan as "an apportioned, delimited share,"
faraḍat / faruḍat al-baqara: the cow grew old and advanced in years — al-Jawharī connects this to the Qur'anic lā fāriḍun wa-lā bikr ("neither aged nor young").
cited from Labīd, "as the Euphrates flows over the outlet of the streamlet."
with a verse from Ṣakhr al-Ghayy, and the note that one must not read the word as qirṣ)
al-farḍ is what God has made obligatory
the science of dividing estates being called farāʾiḍ (ḥadīth: "the most versed of you in farāʾiḍ is Zayd")

al-farīḍa is also the ṣadaqa due on grazing livestock: livestock is said to "become liable to the farīḍa" once it reaches the niṣāb (taxable minimum); the two farīḍatān are the jadhaʿa among sheep and the ḥiqqa among camels.
Core sense — boasting, self-praise.
all mean "praising oneself by listing one's qualities."
Tafākhara (VI): a group vaunt against one another.
Al-fakhkhāra: an earthen jar; plural fakhkhār. Ibn Sīda cites the Qur'an, "from dry clay like the fakhkhār (baked pottery)" (Q 55:14).
Ibn Sīda derives this from sense 1 through Labīd's line about a valley adorned with fākhir herbage: the plant that has reached full, excellent growth, "as though it boasted over what was around it."
Al-Rāghib defines jaʾara as going to excess in duʿāʾ (supplication/calling out) and taḍarruʿ (pleading, self-abasing entreaty)
two root meanings (aṣlān): first, the abundance of a thing and its gathering together; second, the lack of weapons.
al-jamm means "much, abundant", as in Q 89:20, "and you love wealth with an abundant love (ḥubban jammā)".
cites al-Namir ibn Tawlab on a mare "jamūm in her running, her tail raised; you would take the white of her blaze for a lamp"
highlights.note: al-Namir ibn Tawlab, lived into Islam

highlights.text: A ḥadīth says "We were commanded to build the masājid (places of prostration) jumman", which is explained as meaning that their walls should have no crenellations (shuraf).
kashf is raising a thing off whatever conceals or covers it — uncovering, laying bare.
(a) it means kashf, an uncovering (none but God can uncover/remove it)
Poetic witness — Ṣakhr al-Ghayy describes a thundering cloud that "raises a cloak laid bare" for the distant lightning
Used figuratively of war "conceiving out of season" (Zuhayr's verse of the war-mill that grinds, conceives, bears, and bears twins)
Thaʿlab reads it as: none uncovers the Hour but the Lord of the worlds — with the hāʾ intensive.
highlights.note: philologist Thaʿlab's reading of a verse

highlights.text: a literal core of "swallowing down / stopping up / holding in,"
kaẓama l-ghayẓ / kaẓama ʿalā l-ghayẓ — to hold in rage

Al-Zamakhsharī quotes two Qur'anic phrases as examples of exactly this: "when he called out while he was makẓūm," and "his face becomes darkened and he is kaẓīm" — that is, choked with suppressed feeling, on the physical image of the breath being caught.
a line of Ṭarafa comparing drinking the dregs of wine to drinkers gulping the water of a kaẓīma
k-l has three sound root meanings: (1) the opposite of sharpness, (2) one thing surrounding another, and (3) a part of the body.
Kull is a noun coined to express totality, and it is always followed by the word it governs.
He explains kalāla as a verbal noun from takallalahu al-nasab, "the lineage curved round him," which was then used as a name.
He reports the Arab expression "he did not inherit it as kalāla," meaning the inheritance came not from the side but through closeness and right.
According to a report from Jābir ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr said that the heirs of someone who dies with neither child nor parent are kalāla.
Core sense — abundance.
al-kathra (also vocalized al-kithra) and al-kuthr mean the opposite of qilla (fewness).
kātharūhum fa-katharūhum: they competed in numbers and outnumbered them.
the abundant of anything
illustrated by al-Aʿshā's line contrasting mere numbers of "pebbles" with true glory.
dense, massed dust (a Hudhalī usage; verse of Umayya

Ibn Sīda then reports it as the river in the Garden that feeds all its rivers, belonging specially to the Prophet — the referent of «Innā aʿṭaynāka al-kawthar» (108:1) — with a second reported view that al-kawthar there is the good God grants His community on the Day of Resurrection.
**luṭf / laṭaf** = kindness or benevolence (*birr*), combined with subtlety — literally "going unperceived" (*takhaffī*)
*huwa laṭīf bi-l-amr* = he is *rafīq* — gentle, adroit in dealing with it
both meaning to act kindly/gently toward someone
Shāhid — Abū Dhuʾayb: *"nor an intimate, sincere, weeping over me."*
Nidāʾ comes from nadā, moisture.
Nidāʾ is raising the voice so that it becomes manifest.
It can also mean meaningful speech: "when your Lord called Moses" (Q 26:10).

Sitting together came to be called nidāʾ, so a place of assembly is al-nādī, al-muntadā or al-nadiyy, and the words are also used for the people one sits with: "then let him call his assembly (nādiyahu)" (Q 96:17).
Al-Rāghib notes that in the Law the call to prayer is restricted to its well-known wording.
the word nidāʾ is used because he pictured himself as far from God through his sins and bad states, as one who fears His punishment does.
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 19:3

highlights.text: the caller stands for the intellect, the revealed Book, the Messenger, and all the signs showing that faith in God is obligatory.

highlights.text: Core meaning: gathering and assembling.
Town/village (قَرْية) — so named because people gather in it.
al-Nābigha's line about a beast "traversing the low dunes and hillocks."
يرقب / يرتقب / يترقّب = to watch for, await and expect.
Watcher / overseer / scout. رقيب = watcher of a people
أعتق الله رقبته = may God free his neck (person from bondage); "he bequeathed his wealth for [freeing] necks (raqāb)," i.e. slaves.
Proverb of impossibility: "I will not come until the Pleiades meet their watcher" (i.e. never)
Closing shāhid from ʿAdī, describing a horse trailing the dust of wild asses (raqīb al-naqʿ = the trailing edge of the dust)
Core literal sense — moisture/dampness in earth and things
Rain 'moistens' (tharā) the dust/earth; moistened earth is muthran.
Earth that has 'become moist' is tharin
Proverb: 'the two moistures met' — for how quickly two men's affection unites, from the image of fresh rain-moisture meeting the old moisture already in the ground.
'The moisture of water appeared on the horse' = it broke into a sweat — illustrated by a verse of Ṭufayl describing camels' flanks growing damp.
Core sense — holding back, restraining.
وازع العسكر — the officer of an army who holds back whoever pushes forward out of line.
أوزعه الله الشكر — "God disposed him to thankfulness"
Shāhid from Yazīd b. al-Ḥakam al-Thaqafī: he turned back a squadron's charge from a youth whose flesh it had almost left in scattered pieces.
the triliteral pattern signifies "leaving a thing and desisting from it."
khadhala-hu / khadhala ʿanhu — "he withheld his support (naṣr) from him," i.e. abandoned/failed to help him.
khadhūl describes one much given to abandoning others — cited from the Qur'an: "Satan is ever, to man, a khadhūl [forsaker]."
Any "one who leaves" can generally be called khādhil — illustrated with ʿAdī ibn Zayd's image of a bucket whose cross-bars come loose ("are abandoned") and it breaks apart.
God's khidhlān of a servant is glossed as His not shielding him — al-Azharī adds: from wrongdoing, so that he falls into it.
